Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install · [LLM] Editor/AI tool auto-execute config file dropped into project tree by package manager or git
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini spawns interpreter referencing folderOpen or SessionStart hook script · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint · [LLM] Hades on-import payload: python interpreter spawns Bun runtime download · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun runtime egress to npm/PyPI publish endpoints or attacker-controlled GitHub repos
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the 5 SHA256 hashes associated with the Miasma/Hades June 2026 campaign are observed as either an executed binary or a file written to disk on an enrolled host. Catches the worm landing or running irrespective of the delivery vector (npm install, IDE folder open, PyPI import). Rationale: Uses the 5 SHA256 IOCs pre-extracted from the StepSecurity advisory. Cross-checked against Semgrep's Miasma v2 writeup and StepSecurity's Hades campaign writeup which confirm the same hash family. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating IOC in a sandbox VM enrolled to production tenant
  • Defender threat-intel sample auto-downloaded to MpCmdRun quarantine folder
  • Forensic analyst copying the sample to a triage share for review
  • SOAR enrichment pipeline storing the binary in an evidence bucket synced back to disk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\" and FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\evidence\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the host's last 24h DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents and confirm whether the hash was executed (process row) or only landed (file row). Identify the parent (npm.exe, node-gyp, python.exe) and the originating package/folder path. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device in Defender (Isolate Device), force-rotate any npm/PyPI/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure tokens that lived on that host or in any repo the developer recently opened — assume tokens were exfiltrated. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on AccountUpn across all hosts for the same hash, then hunt UC2/UC3 (Phantom Gyp + Hades Bun) against the same user/devices to map full scope; review GitHub for any new workflow files or attacker-controlled repos.
let MiasmaHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (MiasmaHashes)
  | extend Source = "DeviceProcessEvents"
  | project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHashes)
  | extend Source = "DeviceFileEvents"
  | project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in (MiasmaHashes) or Hash in (MiasmaHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImProcessCreate", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileSHA256 in (MiasmaHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImFileEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' technique: a ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped into a package directory under node_modules that triggers code execution at the native build step of npm install, bypassing preinstall/postinstall script monitoring. Filters to package-manager parent processes so legitimate library development is not flagged. Rationale: Article explicitly names the 157-byte binding.gyp as the Phantom Gyp payload dropped during npm install. Size filter (50-500 bytes) plus the node_modules path plus the npm/yarn/pnpm parent are all article-derived; legitimate binding.gyp files in published packages are typically much larger and produced by the package author rather than dropped by tar extraction during install. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer authoring a genuinely tiny binding.gyp stub for a local native addon being tested under node_modules
  • tar.exe extracting a benign package whose author shipped a minimal binding.gyp (e.g. config-only)
  • pnpm content-addressable store unpacking many legitimate binding.gyp files during fresh install
  • Forensic analyst copying a malicious binding.gyp sample to a node_modules path for sandbox testing
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\node_modules\.pnpm\@types\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm publish" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp configure"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: open the file, read its content (it will be small JS/Python embedded inside the gyp action block), and identify the package directory it landed in. Capture the package name + version from the adjacent package.json. Step 2 — Contain: kill any running node-gyp / npm install on the host, isolate the device in EDR, and force-revoke the developer's NPM_TOKEN, GitHub PAT, AWS/Azure/GCP creds, and any tokens visible in process memory of the npm invocation. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the package name across the org to identify other developers who installed the same version; trigger UC1 hash search and UC6 Bun-exfil search; query npm registry for all versions of that package published in the last 7 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\"
| where FileSize between (50 .. 500)   // article: 157-byte Phantom Gyp; allow small obfuscation variance
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe","git.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm i ","npm ci","yarn add","yarn install","pnpm install","pnpm add")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\"
| where TargetFileSize between (50 .. 500)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|git)\.exe$"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm i ","npm ci","yarn add","pnpm install")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma Phantom Gyp - Small binding.gyp Dropped into node_modules
id: 7a1d3c5e-2b8f-4c3d-8e7a-6f4b2d9e1c22
status: experimental
description: Detects creation of a very small binding.gyp file inside node_modules during a package manager invocation, matching the Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' supply-chain worm technique (StepSecurity, June 2026).
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  file_selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\binding.gyp'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\node_modules\'
  size_selection:
    FileSize|lte: 500
  parent_selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\tar.exe'
      - '\git.exe'
  condition: file_selection and size_selection and parent_selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\node_modules\\*\\binding.gyp OR *\\node_modules\\*\\BINDING.GYP) @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\NODE.EXE)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\node_modules\\.+\\binding\.gyp$/i
| WrittenBytes<500
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|tar|git)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, WrittenBytes, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="binding.gyp" Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\*" Filesystem.file_size<500 by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_size Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where match(process_name, "(?i)^(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|git)\.exe$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="binding.gyp" Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\*" Filesystem.file_size<500 by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_size Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where match(process_name, "(?i)^(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|git)\.exe$") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Hades on-import payload: python interpreter spawns Bun runtime download AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades PyPI execution chain: an obfuscated hook in a package's __init__.py runs at import time and fetches the standalone Bun JavaScript runtime (v1.3.13/1.3.14) from GitHub releases or bun.sh, then executes the _index.js payload. Pivot is python.exe as parent of curl/wget/bun or python making outbound HTTP to Bun distribution endpoints. Rationale: Article names the Bun runtime download as the Hades execution mechanism triggered from __init__.py; corroborating writeups (Orca, SocRadar, Rescana) pin the Bun versions to 1.3.13/1.3.14 and the dropper payload filename as _index.js. python -> bun.exe is highly unusual outside this campaign because python developers virtually never bootstrap a Bun runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://orca.security/resources/blog/hades-pypi-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-hades-pypi-supply-chain-attack-poisons-19-python-packages-with-bun-based-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1105 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer experimentally calling out to Bun from a Python script (rare but possible for cross-runtime tooling)
  • Internal data-pipeline using a Python wrapper around a Bun script
  • Anaconda/conda-forge recipe builder fetching Bun as a build dependency
  • Sandbox/dynamic analysis tooling intentionally executing a Hades sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "conda-build" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Anaconda\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enumerate the python process's recent stdin/CWD and resolve which PyPI package was imported. Pull the package's __init__.py, decode the obfuscated one-liner, and confirm Bun download URL. Capture Bun binary SHA256 and the _index.js payload. Step 2 — Contain: isolate device in Defender, kill the bun.exe process tree, force-rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault/Kubernetes tokens for the affected user; revoke any SSH keys present in ~/.ssh. Pull the package version from PyPI; report to PyPI security if not already taken down. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the resolved Bun download IP/URL across all hosts (DeviceNetworkEvents); search for the _index.js payload hash; check for follow-on GitHub repo creations by the user (worm C2 channel).
let HadesPkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools"]);
// Stage A: python parent spawns bun / fetcher referencing Bun distribution
let StageA = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
  | where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","node.exe")
  | where FileName =~ "bun.exe"
      or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux","bun-v1.3.13","bun-v1.3.14","_index.js");
// Stage B: python directly egressing to Bun distribution endpoints
let StageB = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("bun.sh","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, FileName="(network)", ProcessCommandLine="";
StageA
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl="", RemoteIP=""
| union StageB
| order by Timestamp desc
let StageA = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python(3|w)?\.exe$" or ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\py\.exe$"
  | where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(bun|curl|wget|powershell|pwsh|node)\.exe$"
  | where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\bun\.exe$"
      or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","github.com/oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux","bun-v1.3.13","bun-v1.3.14","_index.js")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Source="Process";
let StageB = ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where SrcUsername != "" and Url has_any ("bun.sh","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-x64","bun-darwin","bun-linux")
  | join kind=inner (ImProcessCreate | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python(3|w)?\.exe$" | project DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ProcTime=TimeGenerated, ActingProcessCommandLine) on DvcHostname
  | where TimeGenerated between (ProcTime - 5m .. ProcTime + 5m)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName="python.exe", ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName="(network)", TargetProcessCommandLine=Url, Source="Network";
StageA | union StageB | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades PyPI Worm - Python Spawns Bun Runtime Downloader
id: 9e2f7b1c-4d6a-4f8b-b0c5-7e3d9f1a2b33
status: experimental
description: Detects python interpreter spawning a child process that downloads or invokes the Bun runtime, matching the Hades PyPI campaign's on-import payload (StepSecurity, June 2026).
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\py.exe'
  child_bun:
    Image|endswith: '\bun.exe'
  child_fetcher:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'bun.sh/install'
      - 'github.com/oven-sh/bun'
      - 'bun-windows-x64'
      - 'bun-darwin'
      - 'bun-linux'
      - '_index.js'
  condition: parent and (child_bun or child_fetcher)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\py.exe) (@Image:(*\\bun.exe OR *\\Bun.exe OR *\\BUN.EXE) OR @CommandLine:(*bun.sh/install* OR *github.com/oven-sh/bun* OR *bun-windows-x64* OR *bun-darwin* OR *bun-linux* OR *_index.js*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^python(3|w)?\.exe$|^py\.exe$/i
| (ImageFileName=/\\bun\.exe$/i OR regex("(bun\.sh/install|github\.com/oven-sh/bun|bun-(windows-x64|darwin|linux)|_index\.js)", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("bun.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","node.exe") AND (Processes.process="*bun.sh*" OR Processes.process="*oven-sh/bun*" OR Processes.process="*bun-windows-x64*" OR Processes.process="*bun-darwin*" OR Processes.process="*bun-linux*" OR Processes.process="*_index.js*" OR Processes.process_name="bun.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("bun.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","node.exe") AND (Processes.process="*bun.sh*" OR Processes.process="*oven-sh/bun*" OR Processes.process="*bun-windows-x64*" OR Processes.process="*bun-darwin*" OR Processes.process="*bun-linux*" OR Processes.process="*_index.js*" OR Processes.process_name="bun.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Editor/AI tool auto-execute config file dropped into project tree by package manager or git AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the broader Miasma/Hades tactic of seeding editor and AI-assistant config files into a project so they execute when a developer opens the folder or starts a session. Detects writes of .vscode/tasks.json (runOn:folderOpen), .vscode/setup.mjs, .claude/setup.mjs, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, or .github/setup.js when the writer is git/npm/pip/tar (not the IDE itself) — meaning the file is arriving via a clone or install, not authored locally. Rationale: The article's Table 1 enumerates exactly these 7 file paths and their auto-execute triggers. Pivoting on package-manager/git as the writer eliminates the common FP of a developer manually authoring these files in the IDE — when git clone or npm install drops them, the file came from the published package itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/miasma-mini-shai-hulud-ai-agent-supply-chain-2026/ • https://complexdiscovery.com/when-the-worm-targets-the-assistant-miasma-turns-ai-coding-agents-into-the-trigger/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running git clone on a legitimate repo whose maintainer ships a .vscode/tasks.json for local dev tooling
  • npm install of a package that legitimately includes a .vscode/extensions.json or task config
  • pip install of an internal dev tooling package that ships .vscode files (rare but possible)
  • yarn workspace bootstrap that copies tasks.json from a template directory
  • CI agent fetching repo with .github/setup.js used for environment setup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "git clone https://github.com/<your-org>/" or FolderPath has @"\internal-template-repo\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the dropped file. For tasks.json, look for runOn:folderOpen + node/bun/curl/python invocation. For setup.mjs/setup.mdc/setup.js, examine the JS for obfuscated payloads or fetches to non-corp domains. Identify the originating package (look at adjacent package.json / requirements.txt / git remote origin). Step 2 — Contain: warn the developer NOT to open the folder in VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini; quarantine the file; if already opened, isolate the device, kill any spawned child processes, force-rotate the developer's tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source package name across the org; run UC1 hashes, UC3 (Bun runtime), UC6 (Bun outbound) on the same host; check git log on the repo for who/when added the file.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| extend FullPath = strcat(FolderPath, @"\", FileName)
| where FullPath has_any (@"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.vscode\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
// Drop writes by the legitimate IDE — those are user authoring; keep writes by package managers / git / extractors
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","tar.exe","7z.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git clone","git pull","git checkout","npm install","npm i ","pip install","yarn add","pnpm install")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FullPath, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.vscode\tasks.json", @"\.vscode\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\setup.mjs", @"\.claude\settings.json", @"\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc", @"\.gemini\settings.json", @"\.github\setup.js")
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(git|npm|node|pip|python(3)?|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|curl|wget|bun)\.exe$"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("git clone","git pull","git checkout","npm install","pip install","yarn add","pnpm install")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma/Hades Auto-Exec Editor Config Dropped via Package Manager or Git

status: experimental
description: Detects creation of editor/AI tool config files that auto-execute on folder open or session start, written by git/npm/pip/yarn/pnpm/tar (not by the IDE itself), matching the Miasma/Hades supply-chain delivery surface.
references:

      - '\.vscode\tasks.json'

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\.vscode\\tasks.json OR *\\.vscode\\setup.mjs OR *\\.claude\\setup.mjs OR *\\.claude\\settings.json OR *\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc OR *\\.gemini\\settings.json OR *\\.github\\setup.js)) @Image:(*\\git.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\tar.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\Git.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\Python.exe)

| ContextImageFileName=/\\(git|npm|node|pip|python(3)?|yarn|pnpm|tar|7z|curl|wget|bun)\.exe$/i

VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini spawns interpreter referencing folderOpen or SessionStart hook script AIExploitation High
Detects the moment of execution for the editor/AI-tool auto-execute trigger — Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini parent-process spawning node/bun/python/powershell/cmd with a command line referencing tasks.json, setup.mjs, setup.mdc, .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, or .github/setup.js. This catches the worm running even if the dropping vector (UC4) was missed. Rationale: Article's Table 1 explicitly maps each file to its auto-execute trigger (runOn:folderOpen for tasks.json, SessionStart for .claude/setup.mjs, Custom rules load for .cursor/rules/setup.mdc). When the editor itself is the parent of an interpreter that loads one of these paths, the trigger has actually fired — much higher signal than just the file existing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files • https://hivesecurity.gitlab.io/blog/miasma-mini-shai-hulud-ai-agent-supply-chain-2026/
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's own .vscode/tasks.json running a legitimate build task on folder open
  • Claude Code SessionStart hook running an internal corp-approved setup.mjs
  • Cursor rules file loading a benign internal lint script
  • VS Code Remote SSH bootstrap spawning node for the remote server
  • Anaconda Python environment activation triggered by VS Code Python extension
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has @"\internal-corp-tooling\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--corp-trusted-folder")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: open the referenced setup script (setup.mjs/setup.mdc/tasks.json) and check for obfuscation, outbound fetches, or Bun runtime invocation. Identify the git remote of the project folder. Step 2 — Contain: kill the child process tree, close the IDE, isolate the device. Force-rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault tokens for the developer. Step 3 — Hunt: search across the fleet for the same project path / git remote being opened by other developers. Pivot on UC6 (Bun outbound) to find post-execution exfil. Add the dropped file's SHA256 to the IOC list.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","devenv.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","devenv.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","bun.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","setup.mdc",".github\\setup.js",@"\.vscode\tasks.json",@"\.claude\settings.json",@"\.gemini\settings.json","folderOpen","SessionStart")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(code|cursor|claude|gemini|devenv)\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(node|bun|python(3|w)?|powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|curl|wget)\.exe$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","setup.mdc",@"\.github\setup.js",@"\.vscode\tasks.json",@"\.claude\settings.json",@"\.gemini\settings.json","folderOpen","SessionStart")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime egress to npm/PyPI publish endpoints or attacker-controlled GitHub repos AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma/Hades worm's spreading phase: a Bun runtime instance making outbound HTTPS to npm publish, PyPI upload, or GitHub repo-creation/upload endpoints, indicating either token-driven package republishing or exfiltration to attacker-controlled GitHub repos as documented in the campaign writeup. Rationale: Article and corroborating writeups confirm the worm self-propagates by republishing infected packages (npm publish API, PyPI upload API) using stolen tokens, and exfiltrates harvested credentials through attacker-controlled GitHub repos. bun.exe contacting these endpoints from a developer endpoint (not a CI runner) is high-signal because developers rarely use Bun to drive npm/PyPI/GitHub APIs interactively. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://orca.security/resources/blog/hades-pypi-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567 T1059.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately experimenting with Bun + npm publish for a personal package
  • Bun-based CI tool running publish in a non-CI dev environment
  • Node.js developer using a bun-runtime project that calls GitHub API for legitimate repo management
  • Renovate-bot-style tooling running under node.exe that touches api.github.com/repos
  • Engineer pushing a code snippet to a personal GitHub gist via a Bun script
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Bun\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "renovate"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the bun.exe folder path (was it dropped under %TEMP%, %LOCALAPPDATA%, or a project node_modules?), pull its SHA256 and the parent process. If parent is python.exe or a folderOpen-spawned node, treat as confirmed Hades/Miasma. Step 2 — Contain: block the destination URL at the proxy/EDR network containment, isolate the device, revoke ALL of the developer's npm, PyPI, GitHub, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault, and Kubernetes tokens — the article specifies these are the harvested targets. Audit GitHub for any repos created by the developer's PAT in the last 24h (worm exfil channel). Step 3 — Hunt: check the npm/PyPI registry for any package versions published by the developer's accounts in the suspect window; treat any such publication as a worm-spread event and request takedown. Run UC1, UC3, UC5 across the fleet for the same user.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun.exe","node.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/publish","registry.npmjs.org/-/user","upload.pypi.org/legacy","api.github.com/user/repos","api.github.com/repos","api.github.com/gists")
   or (RemoteUrl has "api.github.com" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("_index.js","bun-","setup.mjs"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/publish","registry.npmjs.org/-/user","upload.pypi.org/legacy","api.github.com/user/repos","api.github.com/repos","api.github.com/gists")
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(bun|node)\.exe$"
    | project DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ProcTime=TimeGenerated
  ) on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ProcTime - 30m .. ProcTime + 30m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra npm supply chain: easy-day-js postinstall dropper (node setup.cjs --no-warnings) AIInstallation High
Detects the easy-day-js@1.11.22 postinstall hook spawning the obfuscated setup.cjs dropper via Node.js with the --no-warnings flag. This is the entry point execution on any developer workstation or CI/CD runner that resolved the poisoned mastra/@mastra packages. Rationale: Anchors on the exact strings published by Microsoft for the malicious postinstall — node binary spawning setup.cjs with --no-warnings (Block 1 of the article). Also restricts the parent to npm/node/yarn/pnpm lineage to slash FPs from unrelated scripts that share the filename. Cross-referenced the mastra GitHub issue 18046 which confirms the postinstall hook in easy-day-js@1.11.22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046 • https://www.linkedin.com/posts/microsoft-threat-intelligence_microsoft-has-identified-a-supply-chain-attack-activity
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546.016 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal npm package whose postinstall is also named setup.cjs and invokes node --no-warnings (rare — the dual-string match makes this unlikely)
  • Developer manually testing/reverse-engineering the malicious dropper after the campaign was disclosed
  • A CI/CD job that intentionally runs a script literally called setup.cjs with warnings suppressed
  • Security tooling (EDR sandbox, npm audit replays) that re-executes the dropper for analysis
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4","c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638","cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066","9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9","221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host (parent npm/yarn → node setup.cjs); collect the SHA256 of the setup.cjs file and compare to the five published hashes; check $TMPDIR for .pkg_history and .pkg_logs markers. 2) Contain: isolate the host or CI runner from network, kill node tree, quarantine node_modules/easy-day-js, rotate every credential / token / SSH key / cloud key that touched that machine since 2026-06-16 07:05 UTC. 3) Hunt: query all hosts that ran npm install/update against the mastra or @mastra scope or that resolved easy-day-js@1.11.21 or 1.11.22 between 2026-06-16 and 2026-06-17; pivot to UC2/UC3/UC5 to confirm second-stage and persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\easy-day-js\", "easy-day-js/setup.cjs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "setup.cjs" and CommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ProcessId
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra C2 beacon: node.exe to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92:8000 / .123:443 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the setup.cjs dropper or its second-stage tasking client connecting to the attacker-controlled Hostwinds infrastructure used by the Mastra campaign. Single-event alerting on the two confirmed C2 IPs. Rationale: Two attacker-controlled IPs (23.254.164.92:8000 fetch, 23.254.164.123:443 beacon) and two Hostwinds DNS names published verbatim by Microsoft Threat Intelligence. Single-IOC match is high-fidelity because the IPs sit on a low-reputation hosting provider and were freshly stood up for this campaign. The DNS join catches detections even when the proxy resolves IPs locally. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel sandbox or red team detonating the dropper for research
  • Security researcher pivoting against the Hostwinds IP space from a corporate host
  • A different legitimate Hostwinds-hosted customer reusing the same IP after take-down (low — IPs were burned)
  • DNS scanner / passive DNS collector hitting the hwsrv-132778x hostnames
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe), pull bytes-up/down to gauge whether the second-stage payload was retrieved or implant beacons completed; enrich the IP via passive DNS for any other Hostwinds C2 names. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.0/24 at the egress proxy / firewall, sinkhole the two hwsrv-132778[56].hostwindsdns.com domains, isolate any host that connected. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source host to UC1 (setup.cjs execution), UC3 (NvmProtocal Run key), UC5 (wallet/browser data access); broaden lookback to 30d to catch any earlier connection from CI runners.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | where RemotePort in (8000, 443)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where AdditionalFields has_any ("hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| sort by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DestinationIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication),
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Name in~ ("hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra implant Windows persistence: NvmProtocal Run key + NodePackages drop AIInstallation High
Detects the cross-platform tasking implant installing login persistence on Windows by writing the NvmProtocal value under HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run and/or dropping protocal.cjs under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Rationale: Microsoft Table 2 names the persistence artifact 'NvmProtocal' (note the typo — 'Protocal' vs 'Protocol') under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\ — both strings are unique enough that any hit is essentially confirmed malicious. The typo is a high-fidelity anchor because legitimate NVM uses 'Protocol' or no such key at all. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user installs a legitimate NVM4W variant that coincidentally writes a similarly named key (extremely unlikely with the 'Protocal' typo)
  • Security tooling re-detonating the implant in an analysis VM
  • Forensic acquisition tooling reading the key (would show ActionType=RegistryQuery, not Set/Created — already filtered)
  • Manual analyst remediation activity touching the path after IR is underway
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","msiexec.exe") or RegistryValueData has "protocal.cjs"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the value data to confirm it points at protocal.cjs; correlate to the initiating process (expect node.exe, sometimes powershell.exe); hash protocal.cjs and compare against the published five SHA256s. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Run value and the NodePackages folder, kill the implant process, rotate any credentials/tokens/cookies accessible to that user. 3) Hunt: query ImageLoadEvents / DllInjection for reflective .NET loads from node.exe in the prior 24h; check for the equivalent macOS LaunchAgent ~/Library/NodePackages/com.nvm.protocal.plist and Linux ~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/nvmconf.service across the fleet.
union
(DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValueName =~ "NvmProtocal"
        or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\ProgramData\NodePackages\", "protocal.cjs")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "protocal.cjs" or FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| sort by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValue =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\ProgramData\NodePackages\", "protocal.cjs")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where TargetFileName =~ "protocal.cjs" or TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages\"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra implant credential access: node.exe reading crypto wallet extensions / browser History AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the second-stage tasking implant inventorying the 166 cryptocurrency wallet browser-extension IDs and copying browser History/Login Data into temp paths prefixed with 'browser-hist-'. Non-browser Node.js process touching browser profile data is the key signal. Rationale: Article confirms node.exe inventories 166 wallet extension IDs across Chrome/Edge/Brave profiles, copies History SQLite into temp paths prefixed 'browser-hist-' (verbatim). Non-browser process reading browser secret stores is normally rare; the node.exe-as-initiator pivot makes this a tight detection on developer endpoints.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005 T1217
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron-based developer tools (VS Code extensions, GitHub Desktop, Slack desktop) reading their own Chromium profile under User Data — distinguish via the Local Extension Settings/History/Login Data sub-paths
  • Browser-history exporters (e.g. browsing-history-export CLI) that some devs run via node
  • Backup/sync tools written in Node that snapshot the browser profile
  • Penetration-testing tooling on engagement laptops
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","code.exe","GitHubDesktop.exe","slack.exe","Teams.exe","Discord.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of node.exe (expect npm postinstall lineage from UC1, not VS Code / Electron); enumerate which extension IDs / which browser profile were touched; check for outbound POSTs to UC2 IPs within 5 minutes of the access. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate node tree, rotate seed phrases / hardware-wallet PINs / exchange API keys / 2FA seeds for every wallet found, expire all browser sessions for that user. 3) Hunt: correlate the user's Okta/Entra sign-ins and CEX exchange logins for the prior 7d; check for fund-movement events; pivot to UC2 for exfil confirmation and any HTTPS POST with the legacy IE8 User-Agent.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Extensions\",
                              @"\User Data\Default\History",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Login Data",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Cookies",
                              @"\Brave-Browser\User Data\",
                              @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\"))
   or FileName startswith "browser-hist-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Extensions\",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\History",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Login Data",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Cookies")
   or TargetFileName startswith "browser-hist-"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) (@TargetFilename:(*\\User\ Data\\Default\\Local\ Extension\ Settings\\* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Extensions\\* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\History* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Login\ Data* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Cookies*) OR @TargetFilename:*\\browser-hist-*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i (TargetFileName=/\\User Data\\.*\\(Local Extension Settings|Extensions|History|Login Data|Cookies)/i OR TargetFileName=/\\browser-hist-/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Mastra implant discovery: PowerShell child of node.exe running Get-StartApps / Get-AppxPackage AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the implant's host-fingerprinting step: enumerating installed software via Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage, and registry Uninstall keys in rapid succession spawned as a child of node.exe. Rationale: Microsoft's Phase 6 reconstruction names the exact three enumeration mechanisms (Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage, registry Uninstall) used by the implant for victim profiling. PowerShell as a child of node.exe is rare in normal developer use; combined with these three discovery commands, this is essentially confirmation of the implant being active.
ATT&CKT1518 T1518.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An npm package's postinstall that legitimately queries installed apps via PowerShell (rare but exists for some Windows-targeting npm modules)
  • node-based system inventory tools (e.g. systeminformation library wrappers) that shell out for AppX data
  • DevOps tooling that uses node to drive PowerShell-based Windows configuration checks
  • Electron app updater that queries Get-AppxPackage to detect Store-installed versions
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "systeminformation" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("electron.exe","Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent node.exe command line; check if setup.cjs or a randomly named .js was the parent (UC1 lineage); look at the next 60 seconds of process events on the same host for follow-on PS reading browser data or registry hives. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node and powershell trees, quarantine any .js dropped under temp/AppData. 3) Hunt: pivot on UC2 (C2 IPs) and UC5 (wallet/browser access) for the same DeviceId; check whether the user has any privileged AD / cloud roles and freeze them pending review.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-StartApps","Get-AppxPackage",@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Get-StartApps","Get-AppxPackage",@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Mastra Implant Host Software Inventory via PowerShell Child of node.exe
id: d40bf617-ae5b-4c2d-bf80-4b9e2f5d6071
status: experimental
description: PowerShell child of node.exe running Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage or reading Uninstall registry keys — host-fingerprinting step of the Mastra/easy-day-js implant.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: ThreatHunting-Now
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1518
  - attack.t1518.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\node.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Get-StartApps'
      - 'Get-AppxPackage'
      - '\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Electron-based installers that shell out to PowerShell for software discovery (uncommon)
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*Get-StartApps* OR *Get-AppxPackage* OR *\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^node\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/(Get-StartApps|Get-AppxPackage|\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","node") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="*Get-StartApps*" OR Processes.process="*Get-AppxPackage*" OR Processes.process="*\\Uninstall*") by Processes.user Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort 0 - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","node") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="*Get-StartApps*" OR Processes.process="*Get-AppxPackage*" OR Processes.process="*\\Uninstall*") by Processes.user Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort 0 - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf"]);
union

        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)

                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )

CryptoBandits scheduled task creation via XML import to Public\Documents 5-char staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects the worm/stealer persistence step where schtasks.exe imports a task definition XML from a 5-character subfolder of C:\Users\Public\Documents. This is the exact persistence shape Microsoft published for CryptoBandits.A and is not produced by legitimate scheduled-task workflows. Rationale: Article code block 1 ships this exact regex verbatim — schtasks.exe + /create + /xml pointing into a [a-z]{4,6} subfolder of Public\Documents is the published CryptoBandits persistence signature and has effectively zero legitimate cause.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software-distribution tools that stage tasks via XML in Public\Documents (rare)
  • IT scripts that import scheduled tasks for shared workstations from a public staging share
  • Backup/imaging utilities that recreate scheduled tasks during post-deploy
  • Custom developer test harnesses validating schtasks /xml syntax
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine, the XML file at the referenced path (Defender DeviceFileEvents on FolderPath), and the parent that spawned schtasks.exe — a wscript.exe/cscript.exe parent is high confidence CryptoBandits. 2) Contain: isolate the device with MDE Live Response, terminate any ugate.exe / wscript.exe with parents in Public\Documents, and pull the XML + the JS payloads from the staging folder. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for ugate.exe execution, curl with --socks5-hostname, cfile under Public\Documents, Defender exclusion adds, and look for the same 5-character folder pattern on other endpoints (USB worm spread).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Curl over Tor SOCKS5 proxy at localhost:9050 to .onion C2 AICommand & Control High
Detects curl.exe being driven through the bundled Tor SOCKS5 proxy at 127.0.0.1:9050 with an .onion destination on the command line. This is the canonical C2 invocation shape for the CryptoBandits clipper /route.php, /recvf.php, and /stub.php endpoints. Rationale: Lifted from article code blocks 2 and 3 — curl.exe with --socks5-hostname localhost:9050 AND a .onion target on the same command line is unique to the malware's documented C2 flow; no legitimate Windows admin workflow co-locates these three tokens.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user manually running a curl-over-Tor command to test the local SOCKS5 listener
  • Red-team C2 tooling using the same Tor SOCKS5 pattern in an authorised exercise
  • Researcher fetching darknet IOC feeds via local Tor client
  • Privacy-conscious user driving curl through Tor Browser's SOCKS port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe", "tor-browser.exe", "firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessFileName — a wscript.exe/cscript.exe parent from C:\Users\Public\Documents is high confidence; capture the full .onion URL for IR notes. 2) Contain: isolate via MDE Live Response, kill curl.exe and any ugate.exe process, and block outbound 127.0.0.1:9050 path is moot — block the parent script and quarantine its folder. 3) Hunt: across the org look for ugate.exe, schtasks.exe importing XML from Public\Documents 5-char folders, cfile creation, and Defender exclusions for that path; treat any second host with the same 5-char folder name as part of the same USB-worm cluster.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("--socks5-hostname", "localhost:9050", ".onion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("--socks5-hostname", "localhost:9050", ".onion")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WScript or CScript executing JavaScript payload from Public\Documents 5-char staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe running a .js file inside the C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js path layout the CryptoBandits worm drops. This is the runtime entry point for the clipper/stealer component that polls the Tor C2. Rationale: Article describes JS payloads dropped to C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js (example given: 'omoho' folder) and executed by Windows Script Host; this combination of path and script host fires only on CryptoBandits-shaped activity.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-management agent dropping a one-off JS troubleshooting script to Public\Documents
  • MSP automation pushing .js fixes through a shared documents path
  • Custom in-house deployment tool using Public\Documents as a staging directory
  • Pentester or red-team operator simulating WSH-based persistence in the same path
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .js file's SHA256 from DeviceFileEvents on FolderPath has 'Public\\Documents' and detonate in a sandbox or strings-scan for 'route.php', 'EVAL', 'SEED', 'PKEY'. 2) Contain: kill wscript.exe / cscript.exe with these arguments, quarantine the 5-char folder, and remove the matching scheduled tasks from UC1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for ugate.exe execution, curl --socks5-hostname, cfile drops, and the originating .lnk on removable media (DeviceFileEvents FileName endswith '.lnk' and FolderPath matches '^[D-Z]:\\').

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed Tor client running as ugate.exe (CryptoBandits bundled proxy) AIInstallation High
Detects execution of a binary literally named ugate.exe — the article's exact name for the renamed Tor proxy that the clipper launches to bootstrap its hidden-service C2. Pair with the binary's location and parent to triage. Rationale: Article names the renamed Tor binary verbatim ('ugate.exe') and notes it is run hidden to bootstrap the hidden-service C2; no legitimate software ships an executable by this name.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app coincidentally named ugate.exe (very unlikely — verify FolderPath and SHA256 first)
  • Red-team operator simulating a renamed Tor client during an authorised test
  • Penetration-testing kit shipping Tor under the same masquerade name
  • Forensics or training lab analysing the same sample on a sanctioned VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Users\\Public\\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\AppData\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FolderPath, SHA256 and the parent process — a wscript.exe parent from Public\Documents is conclusive; submit the hash to the AV cloud and check Defender threat name for CryptoBandits.A. 2) Contain: isolate the device, terminate ugate.exe and its parent script host, and quarantine the binary plus the 5-char staging folder. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for InitiatingProcessFileName == 'ugate.exe' to surface the C2, search across the org for the same SHA256, and check DeviceFileEvents for cfile and the JS payloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\ugate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender exclusion path added for Public\Documents staging folder (worm self-protection) AIInstallation High
Detects the CryptoBandits worm's self-protection step where it adds a Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusion for its C:\Users\Public\Documents staging path before dropping JavaScript payloads. Covers both PowerShell Add-MpPreference and direct registry writes to the Defender exclusion key. Rationale: Article highlights Behavior:Win64/PathExclusion.ST detections and describes the worm excluding its staging folder before dropping payloads; the path string 'Public\Documents' combined with Add/Set-MpPreference + ExclusionPath is article-specific.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP/RMM agent excluding Public\Documents because tenant uses it as a software-drop staging area
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a Defender false positive on a shared workstation
  • Build farm or VDI gold-image script disabling AV scanning of staging directories
  • Endpoint security baseline tool reapplying a curated exclusion list
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "sense.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe", "smc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessFileName + parent chain — a wscript.exe / cmd.exe parent (not Intune/SCCM/admin shell) makes this CryptoBandits; check whether the exclusion is still active via 'Get-MpPreference | select ExclusionPath'. 2) Contain: remove the exclusion ('Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath ...'), isolate the host, and run a full Defender scan over Public\Documents. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (wscript launching .js from the now-unexcluded path), UC4 (ugate.exe), and UC1 (schtasks XML import). Hash-collect anything new found under Public\Documents subfolders.
let ExclusionByPS = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"Public\Documents"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source = "PowerShell", Detail = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let ExclusionByRegistry = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValueName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
   or RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source = "Registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryValueName, " = ", RegistryValueData), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union ExclusionByPS, ExclusionByRegistry
| order by Timestamp desc
let ExclusionByPS = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference")
| where CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where CommandLine has @"Public\Documents"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Source = "PowerShell", Detail = CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
let ExclusionByRegistry = ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValue has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" or RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, SubjectUserName = ActorUsername, Source = "Registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryValue, " = ", RegistryValueData), ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName;
union ExclusionByPS, ExclusionByRegistry
| order by TimeGenerated desc
